tagline: Up Looney Creek through two coal towns to Kentucky's roof.
intro: KY 160 starts at the Looney Creek bridge on the west edge of Benham and follows the creek up its valley through Benham and Lynch, between Looney Ridge and Benham Spur. Then it climbs Black Mountain, all tight bends, to the Virginia line at a gap about 3,700 feet up. The whole run is a little over 10 miles.

Two companies built these towns for coal, International Harvester at Benham and a U.S. Steel subsidiary at Lynch. By the 1940s Lynch had 10,000 people, a hospital and a movie theater. Then mining came to need fewer hands, and in 1996 the rails to both towns were abandoned.

moments.title: Benham
moments.text: International Harvester built Benham as its company coal town, and the town is now a historic district on the National Register.

moments.title: Lynch
moments.text: Laid out by U.S. Steel's coal company in 1917 and named for its head, Thomas Lynch, it sits at 1,716 feet, the highest incorporated city in Kentucky.

moments.title: Black Mountain
moments.text: At the state line a narrow road leads past a radar dome toward the top of Kentucky, 4,145 feet, marked by an old fire tower missing its cab and steps.

practical: KY 160 is signposted closed to tractor-trailers from Lynch to the Virginia line because of its tight bends. The last stretch to the Black Mountain summit is a one-lane dirt road.

sources.label: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Kentucky State and National Scenic Byways and Highways
